What is OpenAI's "Pando"? The Git infrastructure supporting development in the AI era and what teams should consider

As opportunities for AI to write code increase, so do the things development teams need to consider. It is necessary to streamline not just the speed of creating code, but also the flow of saving, testing, and integrating those changes with other tasks.

The "Pando" introduced by OpenAI is an example of the development infrastructure that supports the backend. Reading it from the perspective of "how to handle the changes that AI increases" makes the news easier to understand.
What was announced about Pando
On November 2, OpenAI introduced "Pando," a new backend for Git repositories. A backend is the part that supports the mechanisms users interact with from behind the scenes.

According to the company, Pando is running on OpenAI's monorepo. A monorepo is a method of managing a large amount of code in a single repository. They explain that it is designed to handle parallel writes to numerous branches and massive reads while maintaining compatibility with Git.

It is reported that after the migration, the median wait time for "pushing" changes to a shared destination was reduced by approximately 80%. However, this is a result within OpenAI's environment. It does not mean that your own development time or AI response time will decrease by the same percentage.

Within OpenAI, version control systems were unable to keep up with the scale of parallel work enabled by Codex. As a result of a surge in branch creation, pushes, and merges by engineers and AI agents, system responses slowed down, and reliability reportedly fell below 90%.

As a countermeasure to this challenge, technical details regarding 'Pando', a proprietary Git-compatible backend built by OpenAI, have been released. It is an interesting case study showing what changes are required in infrastructure as AI becomes deeply involved in development work.
Version control challenges brought by the expansion of Codex usage

According to OpenAI's report, Codex has significantly changed the scale and pace of development, enabling engineers to carry out far more work in parallel. This means an increase in branches, pushes, merges, fetches, and clones from development environments and CI (Continuous Integration) jobs.

Existing systems supporting monorepos could not keep up with this surge in demand. This is a case study showing that the scalability of version control infrastructure can become a new bottleneck as development by AI agents becomes commonplace.

When you introduce AI coding, the time spent writing code initially decreases. However, once you start running multiple AI agents simultaneously, other wait times become noticeable: branch creation, pushing, CI, reviews, and merging.

On November 2, 2026, OpenAI released 'Pando,' a Git-compatible backend built for its internal monorepo. Pando itself is not a publicly available product. What we should take away today is not to mimic its design, but to make the decision to verify bottlenecks in the development process with data before increasing AI usage.
What has changed is the 'number of concurrent processes,' not the amount of code

According to OpenAI, Codex has enabled individual developers to work on multiple changes in parallel, increasing the frequency of branches, pushes, fetches, clones, and CI runs. They explained that on their previous infrastructure, fetches and pushes became slow, and there were instances where merge reliability fell below 90%.

Pando is designed to process writes to different branches independently and reuse previously received packfiles during fetches. After the migration, OpenAI reported that it reduced the median push time by approximately 80% and improved merge reliability. This is based on internal performance at a scale that delivers about 1 petabyte of Git data per day.
